card.hook: Here's the catch with the Sky Tower: the best view of it is from anywhere except the Sky Tower. So keep your feet on the ground and let all 328 metres of it show off.
card.stand_here: Stand in Victoria Park, which lies to the west of the tower, and face the tower so it rises above the green lawns with the city high-rises around it. Hold your phone upright, because the tower is much taller than it is wide.
card.zoom: Start at 1x, upright, to fit the tower and the lawns below it. Go to 0.5x for more grass and sky, or 2x if your phone has it, to fill the frame with the shaft and the pod.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the shaft up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean, and leave a little space above the mast so the tip isn't clipped.
card.best_time: Come back in the evening if you can. The tower is lit up for charities and causes, and for New Year fireworks, so it can look very different from your daytime shot. At dusk, try night mode and rest your phone against something solid.
card.selfie_here: Try Te Ara i Whiti (The Light Path), the pink walkway. Stand on the pink path with the tower rising behind you, use the front camera, and try 0.5x to squeeze more of the tower in over your shoulder. A travel guide says it's even better after dark, when the lights change colour. Silo Park in Wynyard Quarter is another option: the grassy areas by the silos, with the tower behind you, in the golden hour before sunset.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Federal Street to take your photo so the tower shows reflected in the nearby glass buildings (it's a single blog tip, so check it on the spot).
card.rules_and_safety: One guide says no selfie sticks on the observation decks, so check with SkyCity before you rely on that. A visitor guide also says straps are required for the open-air SkyWalk and SkyJump, so check what that means for your phone. Going up the tower or joining any activities is separate from visiting the park, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the tower looks as if it's growing out of the lawn, then see if you can get a second one with a tree or lawn in the bottom third.
card.good_to_know: The Sky Tower is 328 metres from ground level to the top of the mast, which makes it the second-tallest freestanding structure in the Southern Hemisphere. It stands at the corner of Victoria and Federal Streets in the CBD, as part of the SkyCity complex. It opened on 3 August 1997, after two years and nine months of building.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Victoria Park, which lies to the west of the tower, and face the tower so it rises above the green lawns with the city high-rises around it. Hold your phone upright, because the tower is much taller than it is wide.

card.hook: You're standing on a grassy volcano, and a whole city is sitting just behind its crater. It's an odd, brilliant combination, and it's the whole reason people climb up here.
card.stand_here: Head to the boardwalk platform closest to the access road, right where the phone icon sits. Face the city, with the crater bowl in front of you and the Sky Tower rising behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole crater and the skyline in one frame, then try 1x for a calmer, more natural view. Zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) picks out the Sky Tower and the city towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the Sky Tower on one of the vertical lines instead of the middle, and keep a strip of grass along the bottom of the frame for depth.
card.best_time: Sunset or sunrise, which several guides single out for photos. The summit is open and exposed, so give yourself a minute or two to line things up.
card.selfie_here: Use the boardwalk platform nearest the summit road, which visitors rate for its views of central Auckland and the Sky Tower. Switch to the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and keep the crater behind you with the city beyond it.
card.rules_and_safety: Please stay on the boardwalk, as it protects the old Māori terraces and storage pits. Paths can be slippery after rain, so stick to marked trails.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the curve of the crater rim leads your eye straight to the Sky Tower. Bonus points if nobody's elbow sneaks in.
card.good_to_know: At 196 metres, Maungawhau is the highest natural point on the Auckland isthmus, and its crater is about 50 metres deep. The name means 'mountain of the whau tree', and it was once an important Māori fortified settlement. The summit road has been closed to most vehicles since 2011, and the boardwalks opened in 2020.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the boardwalk platform closest to the access road, right where the phone icon sits. Face the city, with the crater bowl in front of you and the Sky Tower rising behind it.

card.hook: Picture a 1909 postcard of K' Road, then notice you can stand in almost the same spot and take the same photo. The street still climbs away between the old buildings, just like it did then.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Karangahape Road and Pitt Street and face west along the street. The historic H B Building is on one side, the Naval and Family Hotel is on the other, and the Family Bar sign is far down the road.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the street. Go to zoom 0.5x if you want both rows of buildings and more sky, and keep the phone level so the walls don't lean. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) pulls the Family Bar sign closer and squeezes the street together.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the street's centre line near the middle, tap the far end of the street, and drag it a bit darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Daytime gives the clearest view of the building details. In the evening, switch on night mode and rest the phone against a post or wall to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the K Road overbridge, next to the three bright pop-art banana light poles, which make a fun foreground. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the poles and the street behind you. The address is given as 376 in one place and differently in another, so look for the poles themselves. Another good spot is the stairwell inside St Kevin's Arcade, overlooking Myers Park, which is full of murals.
card.rules_and_safety: Wait for a gap in the traffic and people, and be thoughtful if anyone sleeping rough ends up in your shot. Myers Park, down the steps from St Kevin's Arcade, isn't somewhere to walk alone late at night. Building work for the City Rail Link station near the Upper Queen Street end may change some views, so check on site.
card.challenge: Get the Family Bar sign tiny in the distance while both old buildings frame the street, then compare your shot with a 1909 postcard in your head.
card.good_to_know: Māori used this ridge as a walking route long before Europeans arrived, and it was known as Te Ara o Karangahape, 'The Path of Karangahape'. The road is older than Queen Street. From about 1900 to the early 1960s it was Auckland's busiest shopping street, and in 1935 the whole street was lit with lights under the shop awnings, known as the 'Great White Way'.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Karangahape Road and Pitt Street and face west along the street. The historic H B Building is on one side, the Naval and Family Hotel is on the other, and the Family Bar sign is far down the road.

card.hook: Picture this: you're halfway across a bridge, the colourful silos are lined up ahead, and the whole bridge starts to swing open for a yacht. That's a normal afternoon at Wynyard Quarter, the bit of Auckland waterfront locals still call the Tank Farm.
card.stand_here: Stand on Wynyard Crossing, the bridge over the marina, right at midspan. Face across the marina toward Silo Park, with the city skyline behind the silos.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the bridge, the marina and the skyline in one go. Switch to 1x for a cleaner look at the silos. Then try 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the silos or a single boat.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, use the steel lines of the bridge to lead the eye to the silos, then tap the silos and slide it a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Aim for sunset. Once the sun has gone, switch on night mode.
card.selfie_here: Take a selfie on Wynyard Crossing, where guides rate the view as the area's best waterfront photo spot, or in Silo Park with the old silos behind you on the grass. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and keep the silos over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo on the docks in front of the Auckland Fish Market at the North Wharf end, with you in front and boats moving past behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge lifts for tall boats, so leave a few spare minutes if you need to cross. Crossing on foot is free. If you're walking the Quarter, bring sun protection, comfortable shoes and water.
card.challenge: Catch the bridge mid-swing with a yacht gliding through, and keep the railings dead straight while you do it.
card.good_to_know: Wynyard Quarter is reclaimed land on the Waitematā Harbour, and its last section, Wynyard Wharf, was finished around 1930. For decades it was mostly port land and fuel tanks. Since 2011 the eastern part has been open to the public, with restaurants, walkways and Silo Park, and working fishing boats and ferries still use the docks.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Wynyard Crossing, the bridge over the marina, right at midspan. Face across the marina toward Silo Park, with the city skyline behind the silos.

card.hook: Picture a pale, temple-like building sitting on top of a hill, with the harbour spread out beside it. That's the Auckland War Memorial Museum, and it knows how to make an entrance.
card.stand_here: Head for the forecourt in front of the museum and stand at the Cenotaph. Face the museum so the memorial sits in front of the big building. Turn around for a second shot looking out over the harbour toward Rangitoto Island.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the Cenotaph and the whole museum in one frame. Then try 1x for a calmer, less stretched look. Zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) brings Rangitoto closer or picks out the carved reliefs.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pale stone, then drag the slider to make it a little darker so the walls keep their detail and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters pale stone. Check the sky and the shadows on the front of the building when you arrive.
card.selfie_here: Go up the broad entrance steps and stand between the tall stone columns. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the columns and building rise behind your shoulder. Keep the selfies here and not at the Cenotaph.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Domain Drive to take your photo with the Robert Burns Statue in front and the museum beyond it; it comes from an old photo record, so check it still works on the day.
card.rules_and_safety: The Cenotaph is a place of remembrance, so keep your photos there respectful and skip the posed or playful shots. Check the official site for opening times and any photography rules inside.
card.challenge: Zoom in and find the carved reliefs of the armed forces, then see if you can get one sharp, straight-on shot without a lean.
card.good_to_know: Auckland War Memorial Museum (Tāmaki Paenga Hira) was built as a museum and a memorial to those lost in the First World War. Building began in 1925 and it opened in 1929. The walls are mostly Portland stone, with reliefs by Richard Gross.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the forecourt in front of the museum and stand at the Cenotaph. Face the museum so the memorial sits in front of the big building. Turn around for a second shot looking out over the harbour toward Rangitoto Island.

card.hook: Here's the twist: the best part of Auckland's underground train station is above ground. That grand Edwardian front is the old Chief Post Office, and it looks great next to the busy modern interchange.
card.stand_here: Stand on Lower Queen Street, opposite the Chief Post Office facade near the station entrance. The station lies to the south-east of this spot, so face the building and put the entrance near the middle of your picture.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole facade. If you're too close, tap 0.5x. Try 2x or more to pick out the carved details or the entrance (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the building up with them so the vertical edges stay straight, and hold your phone level so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Check the light on the day and pick the moment when the front is evenly lit. People walk in and out all day, so take a few frames and keep the one with the cleanest foreground.
card.selfie_here: Try the plant-lined walkway and alleys close to the station, under the strung fairy lights. Travel pages call them a popular evening backdrop, so use the front camera, tap 0.5x to fit more in, and let the lights glow behind you. The Transport Centre itself may not be in the shot here.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site before you go if you want to go inside the station or use a particular entrance.
card.challenge: Take your tidiest frame: entrance dead centre, straight edges on the gridlines, and not a single stray passer-by.
card.good_to_know: Waitematā Station is still labelled Britomart on some maps. The post office dates from 1912, and Auckland City Council bought the old building in 1995 for the new transport centre. The station opened to passengers on 7 July 2003, and Sir Edmund Hillary performed the official opening later that month.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Lower Queen Street, opposite the Chief Post Office facade near the station entrance. The station lies to the south-east of this spot, so face the building and put the entrance near the middle of your picture.

card.hook: Picture a bridge that lifts right in the middle of your photo walk, just to let a tall yacht slide through. That's Viaduct Harbour, and it's a lot more fun than a regular marina.
card.stand_here: Stand on Wynyard Crossing, the bridge to the north of the harbour, and face south across the marina. The yachts are right in front of you, with the Sky Tower and the city skyline rising behind them.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the yachts with the Sky Tower behind. Go to 0.5x to squeeze in more of the basin and sky, or try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Sky Tower or one favourite yacht.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the line of yachts along the lower third with the Sky Tower off-centre, then tap the yachts and make the shot a bit darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: If you can, catch the bridge mid-lift. It frames the marina and the Silo Park silos especially well, and a signal sounds first, so you get a warning. For selfies along the marina promenade, a travel guide says the benches and lookout points are especially good at sunset.
card.selfie_here: Hop onto the deck of the Wynyard Crossing swing bridge (walk Quay Street to reach it). Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the marina behind you over your shoulder. One guide rates this bridge as the best waterfront photo spot. Another good option is a bench or lookout point on the marina promenade, with the moored yachts behind you.
card.ask_someone: After crossing Wynyard Crossing, stand in front of the ANZ Viaduct Events Centre and ask a passer-by to take your photo with the marina and Viaduct waterfront in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge opens for tall yachts and a signal sounds before it lifts, so wait on the bridge until the signal finishes and it has stopped moving. Watch your footing on the bridge, and keep your phone low and steady near the water.
card.challenge: Switch on Live Photo while the bridge lifts, then scroll through afterwards and pick your best frame.
card.good_to_know: Viaduct Harbour is a former working harbour, once known as Viaduct Basin and laid out like the basins common in London. For much of the 20th century it was the centre of Auckland's fishing industry, and a mechanical bridge was raised to let the fishing boats in. It later became the hub of the 2000 America's Cup.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Wynyard Crossing, the bridge to the north of the harbour, and face south across the marina. The yachts are right in front of you, with the Sky Tower and the city skyline rising behind them.

card.hook: This isn't a pretty-postcard spot, and that's the fun of it. You stand in a windy, noisy park right under a motorway bridge and look up at steel girders marching off towards the city.
card.stand_here: Stand in Stokes Point Reserve on the north side, directly beneath the bridge. The bridge lies to the south-west, so face that way and look up, with the city skyline across the water.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the whole upward sweep of the bridge, then switch to 1x for a calmer shot. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the city skyline closer between the piers.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the steelwork, then slide it a little darker so the sky keeps some colour, and use the gridlines to keep the piers straight.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the steelwork. At dusk, try night mode with your elbows tucked in, or rest the phone on something solid.
card.selfie_here: In Stokes Point Reserve, stand almost directly underneath the bridge span, use the front camera at 0.5x and let the bridge tower over your shoulder. For a wider, open backdrop, try the wharf at Northcote Point with the bridge and city behind you.
card.ask_someone: If you wander over to Westhaven Marina, ask a passer-by to stand on the boardwalk promenade facing the bridge while you pose with the yacht moorings behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Don't stop or take photos while driving across the bridge; shoot from the park instead. The reserve is very windy, so hold your phone with both hands, keep away from the road, and be respectful if you pass the memorial plaque under the Northcote end.

card.good_to_know: The original four lanes opened in 1959, and two more lanes were added to each side in 1968-1969. The bridge is 1,020 m long. Its main span rises about 43 m above high water so ships can pass underneath.

card.hook: Here's a city corner where a stone château and a modern timber-and-glass extension sit side by side, and nobody seems to mind the age gap. The old half, with its arched windows, is the one your photo wants.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Kitchener Street and Wellesley Street East, at the corner of the original stone building. Face east towards the gallery so the arched windows and a bit of city street fill your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the corner view. If the pavement or traffic stops you stepping back far enough, switch to zoom 0.5x to fit the whole facade in.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the building's corner up with one of the vertical lines, so the stonework doesn't lean. Hold your phone level too, because tilting it up makes the building look like it's falling backwards.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the facade is evenly lit and the street is fairly quiet. Soft daylight flatters the old stone much more than harsh midday sun.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Kitchener Street entrance courtyard and stand in front of the main doors, under the big kauri columns. Use the front camera at arm's length (zoom 0.5x if your phone has it for the front camera) so the gallery sits right behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Up in Albert Park, at the spot overlooking the east sculpture terrace, ask a passer-by to take your photo with the gallery building below you.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the gallery, selfie sticks, flash and extra lighting aren't allowed without the gallery's permission, which has to be requested and granted in advance. Outside on the street you can skip all that.
card.challenge: Do the one-block challenge: get the stone château corner, then walk round and snap the timber-and-glass extension. Two buildings, two moods, one block.
card.good_to_know: The original building dates from 1888, which makes it the first permanent art gallery in New Zealand. It started out sharing its walls with the public library. Today the collection holds more than 18,000 artworks, and the courtyard sculptures change regularly, so what you see may not match the pictures online.

card.hook: You're standing inside an old volcano, and the prettiest thing in it is a tidy pond with marble statues. Auckland Domain is huge, so forget the whole park and go for one scene.
card.stand_here: Stand at Domain Wintergardens, in the central courtyard between the two glasshouses. Face the formal pond so the glasshouse domes frame the view and the glasshouses sit behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the pond and both glasshouses in one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer look at the statues, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for a statue against the glass domes.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the glasshouse roof, then slide the brightness down a little (darker) so the bright glass doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the light is soft and fewer people are about. Sun hitting the glass roofs is a lovely moment too.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the terrace steps that lead down to the central lily pond, with the Victorian statues around you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold it a bit high so the courtyard fits in behind you. For a second selfie, climb the museum's broad steps with the city skyline behind you, ideally at sunset.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the lawn or path in front of the Auckland War Memorial Museum while you stand by the Cenotaph in the museum gardens.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine in the courtyard and other public areas, but they can be restricted inside the glasshouses, so keep your shots outside unless a sign says otherwise. Check the official site for current Wintergardens opening times, and keep paths clear for other visitors.
card.challenge: Crouch down until a marble statue stands against the glass domes instead of the sky, then see if you can get the pond dead centre too.
card.good_to_know: Auckland Domain is the city's oldest park, with 75 hectares of lawns, sports fields, old trees and ponds. It sits inside the remains of a volcano called Pukekawa, which erupted about 100,000 years ago, and the museum stands on the old crater rim. Today the park's official name is Pukekawa / Auckland Domain.

card.hook: Most museums make you go inside for the good stuff. Here, the entrance is the show: a 1920 heritage building stitched into a modern museum, with the harbour behind it.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Quay Street and Hobson Street, right by the museum entrance. From the Viaduct Harbour area it's to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot. Face north-west towards the museum.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole entrance block and a slice of harbour. Then try 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look, and 2x for details on the old facade.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the facade up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Daylight is best, and softer morning or late-afternoon light often looks kindest on the facade. Weekdays and early hours are usually quieter on the waterfront.
card.selfie_here: Head to the outdoor pier beside the museum and pose next to the moored ships, like the Polynesian waka or the Ted Ashby scow. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a bit low so the boats fit in over your shoulder.

card.good_to_know: The Launchman's Building went up in 1920 and got a Category II heritage listing in 1981. The museum opened in August 1993, and its building won an Auckland Architecture Award in 2010. KZ1 was built for the 1988 America's Cup and given to the museum in 1990.

card.hook: Queen Street is almost three kilometres long and close to dead straight, which makes it a gift for a phone camera. The whole street fits in one frame and still looks tidy.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner where Victoria Street meets Queen Street, on whichever side has the clearest view on the day. Face south and look down the length of Queen Street.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the long view down the street. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to squeeze the buildings closer together, or 0.5x if you want the buildings above the street in the shot too.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the street in the middle of the frame, and keep your phone level so the buildings lean in evenly on both sides.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer, and soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the building fronts. Whenever you go, wait for a gap in the crowd and stay on the footpath.
card.selfie_here: Try the Queen Street intersection beside Farmers, which a travel page names as a Queen Street viewpoint with the Sky Tower visible. It doesn't say which way to face, so check that Queen Street is behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and tuck the street over your shoulder. The Waihorotiu Path alongside Queen Street is also recommended for street photos.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is described as fine for personal use, but respect private property and avoid intrusive photos of individuals. It's a very busy street, so work quickly and stay out of people's way. Check the official site for road works or closures before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a liquidambar or Nīkau palm in the foreground with the whole street leading away behind it, and add a few people for scale.
card.good_to_know: Queen Street is named after Queen Victoria and was part of the early town, founded in 1840. In 1902 it became the first asphalted street in New Zealand, and electric trams ran along it until 1956. The footpaths were widened and relaid in a 2006-2008 upgrade, which brought in the new trees.

card.hook: The Town Hall wears two outfits at once: a dark, heavily textured stone base with pale Oamaru limestone stacked on top. Your phone will love the contrast.
card.stand_here: Stand in Aotea Square, just north of the Town Hall, and face south toward the building. Keep a strip of the paved square at the bottom of your frame for a sense of space.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole front and the clock tower in. If you're close and the tower gets cut off, try 0.5x. Then go 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the clock and the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pale stonework, then slide it a little darker so the limestone and the sky both keep their detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer on the pale stone. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your elbows against something steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the antique-style lamplights on Aotea Square, where the Town Hall fills the background. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the building over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in Aotea Square, north-west of the Town Hall and facing south-east toward it, while you stand in front of them with the building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Aotea Square is an open public space, but events can put stalls or stages in the way, so check what's on that day.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines and get the clock tower perfectly upright against a vertical line, with the dark-to-pale stone join in the frame.
card.good_to_know: The Town Hall was designed by Melbourne architects JJ & EJ Clark and opened on 14 December 1911. Its clock tower is 40 metres tall. Inside, the Great Hall seats 1,673 people and houses the country's largest organ.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Aotea Square, just north of the Town Hall, and face south toward the building. Keep a strip of the paved square at the bottom of your frame for a sense of space.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the gateway and the whole square into one frame. Then try 1x for a calmer, more natural look, and 2x or higher (depending on your phone) for the statue or the carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the gateway, then slide the brightness down a little if the sky is bright, so the carving keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Come when it's quieter if you want fewer people wandering through your shot. Or use them to show how big the square is. Dusk is a lovely time to be under the floating sculpture.
card.selfie_here: Pop to the Waharoa at the Queen Street entrance, switch to the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the carved gateway over your shoulder. For a second one, stand on the open plaza under the Neil Dawson 'Mountains and Valleys' sculpture, ideally at dusk.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an open public square, but events can change what's on show, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the crescent moon and the stars on the gateway, then get them in the same frame as your best grin.
card.good_to_know: The gateway is by Māori sculptor Selwyn Muru and is a modern take on a traditional entry gate. Aotea Square opened in 1979 and finished a redevelopment in November 2010. It's designed to hold crowds of up to 20,000 people for concerts, markets and gatherings.

card.hook: The Civic was built to feel like an open-air garden under a twinkling night sky, but out on the corner it's buses, shoppers and city bustle. Don't fight it. That busy street is part of the picture.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Queen Street and Wellesley Street West, outside the main entrance. The theatre is to the west, so face it and let both street frontages frame the corner and the front doors.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the corner and entrance. If the building won't fit from the pavement, tap 0.5x. Go to 2x or higher for details up on the top of the facade.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line up the corner of the building with one of the vertical lines so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Just wait for a gap in the foot traffic, or let a few passers-by add a sense of scale. Evenings bring lit-up shopfronts and a show crowd, so check what's on first, and use night mode with your elbows tucked against your body.
card.selfie_here: On the pavement at the corner of Queen Street and Wellesley Street West, turn your back to the theatre so the facade and its frieze of dancing cherubs are over your shoulder. Use the front camera, or try 0.5x to squeeze more building in. If you have a ticket, the foyer is the other option: stand with the seated Buddhas and twisted columns behind you before the show starts.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't allowed inside the theatre. The interior is only open with a ticket or at set times, and photo rules vary, so ask staff first. Step back only as far as is safe from the traffic.
card.challenge: Catch a stranger walking past the entrance while the corner of the building sits perfectly straight on your gridline, then spot the dancing cherubs.
card.good_to_know: The Civic opened on 20 December 1929 and seats 2,378 people. It's the largest surviving 'atmospheric' cinema in Australasia, and it reopened in 1999 after a two-year restoration. Its interior also appeared in Peter Jackson's 2005 film King Kong.

card.hook: Here's a funny thing about the Ferry Building: it's the old-timer on the shoreline, and the shiny modern Cloud building is parked right beside it. Get both in one picture and you've captured Auckland's waterfront in a single frame.
card.stand_here: Walk down from the top of Queen Street to the waterfront. The Ferry Building is to the south-west, about 5 minutes on foot. Step onto Queens Wharf, the pier just along the waterfront, and face the Ferry Building, with the water and the Cloud building beside it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the building, the water and the Cloud all fit. If you're close and the building won't squeeze in, drop to 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for a tighter shot of the façade.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the building up with a vertical line so it stands straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Early morning or later in the afternoon is a good bet, when the light is softer. Work has been reported around the building, so have a quick look at conditions when you arrive.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and switch to 0.5x so there's room for the Ferry Building over your shoulder. Hold the phone a little higher and tilt it so the building isn't cropped out.
card.rules_and_safety: Work has been reported around the building in the past, so check current conditions when you arrive. If a barrier or crane spoils one angle, move a few steps along the wharf and try again.
card.challenge: Get the old Ferry Building and the modern Cloud building in the same shot, with a strip of water in front, and see if you can keep the building perfectly straight on the gridlines.
card.good_to_know: The Ferry Building sits on Auckland's waterfront at the harbour end of the city centre. Heritage New Zealand has a photo set showing it framed from Queens Wharf. A visitor guide lists the wharf as a free place for harbour and waterfront photos. For a head-on view of the façade, walk to the top of Queen Street where it meets the waterfront. It makes a good second picture.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk down from the top of Queen Street to the waterfront. The Ferry Building is to the south-west, about 5 minutes on foot. Step onto Queens Wharf, the pier just along the waterfront, and face the Ferry Building, with the water and the Cloud building beside it.

card.hook: Cherubs riding dolphins, dolphins blowing horns, and a figure of Aphrodite perched on top of it all. Albert Park's cast iron fountain came from Great Britain in 1881, and it's still showing off.
card.stand_here: Stand in the central area of Albert Park, beside the Victorian fountain. The park's middle lies a little to the east from here. Face the fountain so the flowerbeds, mature trees, paths and benches all fall into view.
card.zoom: Zoom 1x for the fountain with the flowerbeds and trees around it. Drop to 0.5x to fit in the whole formal layout, then zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) to pick out the dolphins, cherubs and Aphrodite.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the fountain, then drag the slider to make the picture a touch darker so the sky and the water don't burn out.
card.best_time: Go early morning or late afternoon, when the softer light picks out the fountain nicely. Spring and summer bring colour to the flowerbeds, and cherry blossom and magnolias bloom in spring.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Wellesley Street East footbridge that links the park to AUT. Stand on it facing out over the city centre with the park behind you, then use the front camera at 0.5x to fit in as much as you can.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the University of Auckland side of Princes Street and shoot across the road, while you stand in front of the park so the whole park shows behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: One guide warns that the park's entrances from Queen Street are very steep, and the path from the Bowen Avenue and Kitchener Street corner also climbs steeply, so allow a little extra time for the walk up.
card.challenge: Get the fountain, a curve of path and a bench into one shot, with the fountain sitting right on the centre gridline. Bonus points if the cherubs are still sharp.
card.good_to_know: The park's formal layout of paths and flower gardens has changed little since the 1880s, so it still feels like a Victorian town park. More than 80 tree species were planted here between 1874 and 1908, and some of those trees date from the 1800s. A statue of Queen Victoria (1897) stands north of the fountain, and the bandstand (built 1900-01) is to the south.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the central area of Albert Park, beside the Victorian fountain. The park's middle lies a little to the east from here. Face the fountain so the flowerbeds, mature trees, paths and benches all fall into view.

card.hook: Holy Trinity looks like it couldn't decide which decade to be, and that's exactly why it's fun to photograph. Steep gables, a big window and plain modern lines all squeeze into one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Parnell Road footpath in front of the west façade, near the entrance. The cathedral lies to the east, so face it and you'll see the big entrance window and gabled front straight on.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a straight-on shot. If a passer-by or the narrow footpath won't let you fit the whole front in, switch to 0.5x. Use 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to home in on the gable or the window.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the edges of the façade up with the vertical lines so the walls don't lean, with the window in the middle and a little sky above the gable.
card.best_time: Pick a day with soft, even light so the front has no harsh shadows. Late afternoon may suit the west front best. Early morning or a quieter day should mean fewer people on the footpath.
card.selfie_here: Head to the lawn of Trinity Garden, next to the open side of the chapel and under the oak trees. Use the front camera at 0.5x, with the green of the oaks around you and the cathedral's modern pavilion and neo-Gothic chancel over your shoulder. The exact framing isn't confirmed, so try a few angles on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand at the corner of Parnell Road and Cathedral Place, across the road from the cathedral and St Mary's Church, while you stand on the cathedral side of the road.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working church, so be considerate of anyone coming and going. Photography for personal use is generally permitted inside, but flash may be restricted, especially during concerts.
card.challenge: Catch the old and the new in one shot: a pointy gable and a plain modern wall, with no leaning walls allowed.
card.good_to_know: The older brick and reinforced-concrete neo-Gothic chancel was joined by a modern nave designed by architect Professor Richard Toy. The foundation stone was laid in 1957 and the main church was consecrated in 1973. Beside it stands the wooden St Mary's Church, designed by Benjamin Mountfort and finished in 1897, then moved across Parnell Road in 1982.

card.hook: Over 5,000 roses on one side, a harbour and the Auckland skyline on the other, and only a short stroll between them. It's two photo jobs in one visit.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Fred Ambler Lookout at the lower end of Dove-Myer Robinson Park (walk down through the rose garden to reach it). Face out over the harbour towards the city skyline, with the container terminal below you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, or use panorama, to catch the whole harbour and skyline. Then try zoom 1x with the terminal in the foreground, and zoom 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the city towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the skyline along the upper third and keep the phone level so the water line stays straight.
card.best_time: The roses are usually best from November, when the Parnell Festival of Roses is held, and on into the new year. Outside those months the beds are quieter, but the view stays just as good.
card.selfie_here: Try the White Garden, a popular photo spot inside the rose gardens: use the front camera and hold it a little low so the roses fill in behind you. The lookout shelter is another option for a harbour backdrop, but the roses won't be behind you there, so it's a harbour selfie rather than a rose one.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in front of the distinctive archway entrance to the gardens while you stand under it, so they can frame you with the arch around you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is welcome in the park, and dogs must be kept on a lead. Opening times aren't clear, so check the council page before you go.
card.challenge: Get one rose sharp with the rest of the bed blurry behind it, then walk down and snap the skyline on the top third of your screen. Two shots, one short stroll.
card.good_to_know: Parnell Rose Gardens is the everyday name for Dove-Myer Robinson Park, named after Auckland's longest-serving mayor, who held the job for 18 years. The Nancy Steen Garden opened in 1984 and shows older heritage roses in a softer, cottage-style look. The old timber house that's now the Luxerose cafe dates from around 1905.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Fred Ambler Lookout at the lower end of Dove-Myer Robinson Park (walk down through the rose garden to reach it). Face out over the harbour towards the city skyline, with the container terminal below you.

card.hook: Look up from Federal Street and there's the spire, poking above the surrounding streets like it wants to be in your photo. The stonework fills the frame without crowding it, which makes your job easy.
card.stand_here: Stand in Saint Patrick's Square, in front of the main west facade, and face the entrance. If you're on the street side, walk round the building to reach it.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to get the whole building and both spires in. Switch to 1x for a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the spire and the carved stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the middle of the building up with the centre line, and hold your phone level so the towers don't lean in.
card.best_time: Daylight is easiest for the full building. After dark, try the corner of Hobson Street to see the cathedral lit up with the presbytery in front. Check on the day.
card.selfie_here: Try the pavement on Wyndham Street, with the facade behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and tuck the spires over your shoulder. The exact spot isn't fixed, so wander a few steps until the stonework fits behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by near the corner of Wyndham Street and Federal Street, and stand on the Wyndham Street pavement with the facade behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working place of worship, so keep your voice low, skip the flash, and check the official site for Mass and visiting times before you go inside.
card.challenge: Get both spires perfectly balanced on the middle gridline, with a strip of foreground at the bottom, and no leaning towers allowed.
card.good_to_know: The land was granted to Bishop Pompallier, New Zealand's first Catholic bishop, in 1841. The building you see today was finished in 1907 and opened on 23 February 1908. It's a Category I historic place, and its spire even shows up in the 1988 film The Navigator: A Medieval Odyssey.
